subtype: Approach: root-cause analysis with five whys [Thinking]
passage: I'm Vaibhav, Thomas's roommate, and I was there the night he finally stopped saying "I'm just stupid." He had failed two courses, Signals and Maths III. He sat at his desk with a sheet of paper and wrote "Why did I fail?" at the top. Under it: "Didn't understand the material." Why? "Missed the first four weeks." Why? "I was home in Kottayam. Amma was in hospital." Why didn't you catch up after? He stopped writing for a while. Then: "I was embarrassed to ask the professors. Everyone else seemed ahead." And why didn't you ask anyway? "Because I thought asking meant I wasn't smart enough." He put the pen down and looked at me. "So it wasn't ability. It was four missed weeks and not asking." I don't know exactly what he felt. But he didn't call himself stupid again that semester.

qa.q: Which two courses did Thomas fail?
qa.a: Signals and Maths III.

qa.q: What might Thomas have felt when he wrote the last answer?
qa.a: Thomas probably felt a mix of relief and sadness, seeing that embarrassment about asking, not lack of ability, was behind the failure.

qa.q: What else could Thomas do next semester?
qa.a: Thomas could meet each professor early, especially after any missed weeks, and join a study group so asking for help becomes normal.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav see the change in Thomas?
qa.a: Vaibhav notices Thomas stops calling himself stupid, without claiming to know exactly what he felt.

grounding: Shows a student who failed two courses asking why repeatedly and tracing it to classes missed during a family illness and to not asking for help, not to ability.

subtype: Approach: root-cause analysis with five whys [Thinking]
passage:
Results day, June. Pankaj stared at two red Fs, in Thermodynamics and Fluid Mechanics. "I'm just not engineering material," he told Asif on the hostel stairs.
Three days later. Asif sat with him in the empty canteen with a notebook. "Humour me. Why did you fail?" "I didn't understand the second half." "Why?" "I'd missed the first month." "Why?" "Papa's surgery. I was in Jaipur with him." "Why didn't you catch up?" Pankaj was quiet. "I didn't want to go to the professors. I thought they'd think I was making excuses." Asif wrote it down: "Missed month plus not asking. Not ability."
August. On the first day of the new term, Pankaj knocked on the Thermodynamics professor's door with his notebook. "Sir, I failed last term. I missed the first month. Could you tell me where to begin?" The professor pulled up a chair.

qa.a: Thermodynamics and Fluid Mechanics.

qa.a: Pankaj felt embarrassed and afraid they would think he was making excuses.

qa.a: Asif patiently asks why again and again, helping Pankaj see the failure came from a missed month and not asking, not lack of ability.

grounding: Illustrates a student using repeated whys to trace two failed courses to a month missed for a family illness and to reluctance to ask for help.

subtype: Approach: talking honestly with an academic advisor [Action]
passage: I'm Sharmila, and I went with Deepika to the academic advisor's office because she asked me to wait outside. The door didn't close properly, so I heard most of it. She told her about the part-time job she took when her father's shop closed, the classes she missed, the tests she didn't prepare for. Dr. Menon listened, then got practical. The backlog exams were in the first week of December. Credits from failed courses wouldn't count until cleared. And with three backlogs, she could take a lighter load next term, four courses instead of six. When Deepika came out, her eyes were wet but her shoulders were straighter. She showed me a printed sheet: dates, rules, a plan. She walked faster than when we came.

Monday. Rehana's marksheet showed two failed courses. She put it face down in her drawer and told her brother Varun everything was fine.
Thursday. Varun found the sheet while looking for a charger. He didn't shout. "Go and see your advisor. Take this. Tell her what really happened." That afternoon Rehana sat across from Professor Iyer with the marksheet between them. She explained: the long commute from Thane, the weeks of headaches, the classes she'd stopped attending. Professor Iyer nodded and opened a file. "Backlog exams are on 10 and 12 January. Failed credits carry forward until cleared; you won't lose your year. And next term, I'd like you on five courses, not seven."
February. Rehana passed both backlogs. Her lighter timetable was pinned above her desk. Varun saw it and grinned. "So it was fine." "It is now," she said.

subtype: Approach: avoidance and hiding the result [Pitfall]
passage: Hrithik, you asked why I'm repeating second year. Okay. I'll tell you the whole thing, because I don't want you to do what I did. I'm Siddharth. Last June I failed two subjects. My father had told half the relatives I'd get a distinction. I couldn't say it. So I said nothing. The backlog exam form was due on 15 July. I saw the notice. I told myself I'd fill it after I found the right moment to tell Papa. The moment never came. The deadline passed. Then the next exam cycle filled up before I'd even checked. By December the college told me I couldn't move to third year with those credits missing. Two failed papers became a lost year. And I still had to tell Papa, only now the news was much worse. If you ever fail something, fill the form first. Tell them second.

qa.q: When was the backlog exam form due?
qa.a: On 15 July.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth say nothing?
qa.a: Siddharth was afraid of Papa's reaction, since Papa had told relatives about a distinction, and felt too ashamed to say it.

qa.a: Fill the backlog form before the deadline, then tell the family, perhaps with help from an advisor or a trusted relative.

qa.q: How might Papa feel hearing the news in December?
qa.a: Papa is likely more hurt and worried than he would have been in June, since hiding it turned two papers into a lost year.

grounding: Shows a student who, afraid of the family's reaction, hides the failure and skips the backlog form, so lapsed deadlines make things worse than the original failure.

subtype: Approach: avoidance and hiding the result [Pitfall]

He closed the tab fast. I asked if he was okay. He said, "Just leave it." August came. He didn't register. In September a letter came from the university saying his next attempt would be the following summer, and that he couldn't carry the missing credits into final year. His mother read it at the dining table. I've never heard a room that quiet. I can't know everything he was feeling, but I saw his face. He looked less scared than exhausted.

Wednesday
Four backlogs. I finally stopped panicking and made a list instead.
Zeenat lent me her course map from the department, the one with arrows showing which course you need before which. I copied mine:
Data Structures: needed for Algorithms, Databases AND the final-year project. Big arrow.
Discrete Maths: needed for Algorithms.
Economics elective: needed for nothing.
Technical Writing: needed for nothing, can be cleared any term.
So Data Structures and Discrete Maths block everything. If I don't clear them by next term, I can't take Algorithms, and the whole of fourth year shifts.
The electives can wait a term. It feels strange to leave them, like I'm ignoring a problem. But they aren't blocking anything.
Plan: December backlog exams, only Data Structures and Discrete. Electives in May.
Chaitanya

subtype: Approach: rebuilding routine with small checklists [Action]
passage:
Student mentor's note, Ayesha (second year), week 4 of the new term.
After failing two courses last semester, Ayesha came to me wanting a "total transformation". We agreed on something much smaller: a daily checklist of only three lines. Attend every class. Revise one hour. Solve five past questions. Nothing else counted.
She keeps it on an index card in her phone cover. Her friend Mahima checks in with her at dinner: "How many ticks?"
This week she told me about Tuesday. She'd slept badly, felt low, and didn't want to leave her bed. She almost skipped everything. Then she looked at the card and thought: three things, I can do three things. She went to class, did forty minutes of revision instead of an hour, and five questions. "Not perfect, but not zero," she said.
Next step: keep the list at three until mid-terms. Only then consider adding a fourth.

qa.q: Where does Ayesha keep the checklist?
qa.a: On an index card in her phone cover.

qa.q: How was Ayesha feeling on Tuesday?
qa.a: Ayesha felt low and tired after sleeping badly, and didn't want to leave her bed.

qa.q: What else could help Ayesha keep the list going?
qa.a: Ayesha could note her ticks each week and share them with Mahima or the mentor, so progress stays visible even in messy weeks.

qa.a: Mahima asks about the ticks at dinner, giving friendly daily accountability without pressure.

subtype: Approach: rebuilding routine with small checklists [Action]

Friday
Day 12 of the list. Still three lines on the sticky note above my desk:
1. Go to every class.
2. One hour of revision.
3. Five past-paper questions.
That's it. After last semester's two failures, I wanted to do everything: eight-hour days, colour-coded notes. Darshan said, "You'll quit in a week. Make it so small you can't fail it." Annoying, but he's usually right.
Today was bad. Mum called, worried about fees, I slept through breakfast, and I cried in the washroom before the 10 am lecture. I still went. Did the hour in the library, badly. Did five questions, got two wrong.
Three ticks. On a day like this, three ticks.
I think that's the point of a small list. A bad day can't knock it over.
Gurleen

subtype: Approach: overcorrecting with an extreme schedule [Pitfall]
passage: After failing three subjects in my second year, I decided to punish myself into success. I'm Kamal. I made a timetable with twelve hours of study every day: 5 am to 9 pm, twenty-minute meals, no phone. My roommate Zubin looked at it and said, "That's not a timetable, that's a sentence." I laughed and ignored him. The first week, I nearly managed it. By the middle of the second week I was sleeping through alarms, my eyes burned, and I couldn't remember a thing I'd read. On the tenth day I sat at my desk and felt nothing at all. I closed the book and didn't open another one for eight days. I'd gone from twelve hours to zero. Looking back, the failure wasn't that I was lazy. It was that I planned for a person who doesn't exist.

Semester five, the failed one: he'd been building a website for the local school, late every night, right through exams. "It's not that I can't study," he told Nitin. subtype: Approach: tracking weekly progress and adjusting [Revision]
passage: Yash, you're checking your marks every Sunday? Good. Let me tell you what that did for me, back in my second year of college in Darjeeling, after I'd failed two papers. My roommate Pasang made me a simple chart on the back of an old calendar: attendance and quiz scores, every Sunday, against what I'd promised myself. "Tenzin, you have to look even when it's ugly," he said. For three Sundays the chart showed electronics stuck around 40, however many nights I sat alone with the book. On the fourth Sunday I finally admitted it: studying alone wasn't working. There was a group of four who met in the canteen after classes. I asked if I could join. Six weeks later, electronics was at 62. The chart didn't fix anything, Yash. It just stopped me lying to myself.

qa.q: What did Pasang make?
qa.a: A simple chart on the back of an old calendar.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel on the fourth Sunday?
qa.a: Tenzin felt frustrated but honest, finally admitting that studying alone wasn't working.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made the difference?
qa.a: Choosing, after three flat Sundays, to ask the canteen group to join, instead of more nights alone with the book.

qa.q: How did Pasang see the weekly chart?
qa.a: Pasang saw it as a way to face the truth, insisting Tenzin look at it even when it was ugly.

grounding: Illustrates a student tracking weekly scores against targets and, after three weak weeks in one subject, switching from solo study to a peer group.
